title: Χελιδὼν ⟨κομπάζουσα⟩ καὶ κορώνη
titleEn: The Boasting Swallow and the Crow
part: The Boasting Swallow and the Crow (Chambry 350)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 350. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἡ χελιδὼν ἔφη πρὸς τὴν κορώνην· « Ἐγὼ παρθένος καὶ Ἀθηναία καὶ βασίλισσα καὶ βασιλέως τῶν Ἀθηνῶν θυγάτηρ ⟨εἰμί⟩, » καὶ προσέθηκε καὶ τὸν Τηρέα καὶ τὴν βίαν καὶ τὴν ἀποκοπὴν τῆς γλώττης.
sentences.tr: Hē chelidōn ephē pros tēn korōnēn· « Egō parthenos kai Athēnaia kai basilissa kai basileōs tōn Athēnōn thygatēr ⟨eimi⟩, » kai prosethēke kai ton Tērea kai tēn bian kai tēn apokopēn tēs glōttēs.
sentences.l: The swallow said to the crow: « I ⟨am⟩ a maiden and an Athenian and a princess and the daughter of a king of Athens, » and she added Tereus too, and the violence, and the cutting-off of her tongue.
sentences.i: The swallow said to the crow: « I am a maiden, an Athenian, a princess, the daughter of the king of Athens, » and she went on to bring in Tereus as well, and the rape, and the cutting out of her tongue.
sentences.n: The swallow is Philomela, daughter of Pandion king of Athens: Tereus, her sister's husband, raped her and cut out her tongue so that she could not tell of it, and the sisters were turned into birds. Chambry supplies ⟨εἰμί⟩, 'am', in his angle brackets — Greek can build a sentence out of nouns alone and needs no copula. τὴν βίαν is bare 'the violence', the ordinary word for a rape, and the story is expected to be known. τὴν ἀποκοπὴν τῆς γλώττης puts into two nouns what English wants a clause for.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ κορώνη· « Τί ἄν, ἔφη, ἐποίησας, εἰ τὴν γλῶτταν εἶχες, ὅπου, τμηθείσης, τοσαῦτα λαλεῖς ; »
sentences.tr: Kai hē korōnē· « Ti an, ephē, epoiēsas, ei tēn glōttan eiches, hopou, tmētheisēs, tosauta laleis ; »
sentences.l: And the crow: « What would you have done, she said, if you had your tongue, seeing that, it having been cut out, you chatter so much? »
sentences.i: And the crow said: « What would you have done if you had your tongue, seeing that with it cut out you chatter as much as this? »
sentences.n: Καὶ ἡ κορώνη stands with no verb of its own; ἔφη comes inside the speech instead. ἄν with the aorist indicative ἐποίησας, answered by the imperfect εἶχες in the if-clause, makes the whole thing contrary to fact — she has no tongue. τμηθείσης is a genitive absolute with 'the tongue' left to be picked up from the clause before. ὅπου here is not 'where' but 'seeing that'. The Greek question mark is the semicolon ;, and Chambry prints a space before it.

sentences.t: Ὅτι οἱ ἀλαζόνες διὰ τοῦ λόγου ψευδολογοῦντες αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς ἔλεγχος καθίστανται.
sentences.tr: Hoti hoi alazones dia tou logou pseudologountes autoi heautois elenchos kathistantai.
sentences.l: That braggarts, speaking falsely by means of their talk, are themselves set up as a proof against themselves.
sentences.i: The story shows that braggarts, lying as they talk, become themselves the very proof that convicts them.
sentences.n: A moral in the bare Ὅτι form: the introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek, which begins simply 'That…', and is supplied in the idiomatic line. ἔλεγχος is the proof that puts a man to shame, the thing that convicts him; καθίστανται in the middle is 'are set up as, come to be'. αὐτοὶ ἑαυτοῖς places the boaster on both sides at once — witness and accused together.
